- Model tends to overestimate prices, especially in the early part of the forecast horizon (first 5–10 days).
- Overshoots after sharp upward spikes in history (e.g., after 75–80+ values), then underestimates the subsequent correction.
- Underestimates mean-reverting periods — model holds too much upward momentum, fails to recognize pullback toward prior 30-day average.
- Forecast lags behind true values by 1–3 days in the first 10–15 days, then catches up or slightly overshoots.
- High variance in forecast early on (e.g., >10% deviation from true) often correlates with high volatility in history — model reacts too aggressively.
- Model underestimates downward trends after strong upward moves — fails to recognize “reversal” or “sell-off” triggers.
- Forecast tends to be smoother than true values — misses short-term volatility spikes or sudden drops.
- When history shows a clear peak, model often forecasts a peak followed by a “flat” or “slightly declining” trend, not a sharp correction.
- Model overconfident in early forecast days — often overestimates by 2–5% relative to true outcome, then corrects gradually.
- Horizon-specific: 1–3 day forecasts are most prone to lag, 5–10 day forecasts show most overshoot, 15+ day forecasts show mean reversion bias.
